handbook.first_steps.title: First steps
handbook.first_steps.body:
You govern one country of the real world as it stood on 1 January 2024. Nothing after that day is scripted: prices, wars, borders and governments come out of what every country does.

## The first ten minutes

- The campaign starts paused. Look around first: nothing is lost by waiting.
- Read the top bar. The balance under the treasury says whether the country gains or loses money every week.
- Open Budget on the left rail. Taxes and spending are set there, and every row explains itself when you rest the cursor on it.
- Open Science and choose a research project. Research points are spent every week, and with no project they are wasted.
- Open a region of yours on the map and build something in it. Construction capacity that builds nothing is thrown away.
- Open Diplomacy and look at your neighbours: who likes you, who does not, and the reasons.
- Press Space. Time runs, and the speed buttons 1 to 5 make it run faster.

## Where to look for help

Every button and figure has a tooltip: rest the cursor on it. Every screen has a "?" that opens its page in this handbook, and F1 opens the handbook from anywhere. The situation report on the right lists what needs your attention now, and the first steps under it tick themselves off as you do them.
handbook.top_bar.title: The top bar
handbook.top_bar.body:
The strip across the top is the country in one line. Each figure has a second line under it: how it moved over the last week. Rest the cursor on a figure for what it is made of.

- Treasury: cash in hand, in billions of dollars. It pays for everything the state does.
- Balance: what the treasury gains or loses every week. A red balance is the first thing to fix, because a treasury that runs out means borrowing, and then debt.
- GDP: what the economy produces in a year, priced at today's market. It is worked out from what is actually made, so it moves with factories, workers, shortages and war.
- Inflation: how fast prices rise. Comfortable is around two per cent; the central bank in Budget is the lever.
- Population: everybody living in the regions you own.
- Stability: how settled the country is. Low stability costs output and taxes, and invites unrest, secession and worse. Under it is war support: how far the people back a war.
- Manpower: people who can still be put in uniform, and how many join the reserve a day.

On the right are the date, the Handbook and Menu buttons, the pause button and the five speeds.
handbook.time_and_saves.title: Time, pause and saving
handbook.time_and_saves.body:
The clock runs in steps of game time. Space pauses and resumes it, the buttons 1 to 5 set the speed, and the game pauses on its own when an event or an offer needs your answer (the option "Pause when something happens").

## Saving

- Esc opens the menu, with saving, loading and settings.
- F5 quick-saves and F9 loads the quick-save.
- The campaign also saves itself on a schedule you choose in the settings. Autosaves never overwrite your own slots.

A save holds the whole world: countries, regions, armies on the march, wars, the market and history. A save made on an older map is refused instead of being loaded wrong.
handbook.situation_rail.title: The situation report
handbook.situation_rail.body:
The column on the right is the situation report. At the top are alerts, each a click away from the screen that deals with it: a shortage of goods, nothing being built, a battle, divisions out of supply, inflation running away, decisions you can take.

Below them are groups you can fold away: the first steps for a new campaign, world news, your wars and battles, your navy, the regions you watch, the market and construction. The world news shows what matters - wars, peace, new countries, crises - and anything that concerns your own country. Everything else is kept in Reports.
handbook.map_controls.title: Moving around the map
handbook.map_controls.body:
- Hold the right mouse button and drag to turn the globe or move the flat map.
- The mouse wheel zooms; WASD moves the camera.
- F2 switches between the globe and the flat map. F3 turns map smoothing on and off.
- Left click selects: a country, a region, a division or a battle.
- Drag with the left button to select several divisions; Shift adds to the selection.
- Right click on a province gives the selected divisions a march order; Shift with right click adds a waypoint.
- Right click on another country's land opens its dossier.
- F6 pans the camera slowly for showcases, F10 flies a free camera without the interface.

Close in, the map shows province borders, cities and every counter; far out it keeps only what matters at that scale.
handbook.map_modes.title: Map modes
handbook.map_modes.body:
The buttons in the bottom right corner change what the map shows.

- Political: countries, and who controls what. Occupied ground keeps its owner's colour with the occupier's hatching over it.
- Diplomatic: alliances, guarantees and dependencies, seen from your country.
- Wars: who is fighting whom, the fronts and the ground that has changed hands.
- Population and economy: countries by how many people they have and how large their economy is.
- Terrain: the ground itself. Rest the cursor on a province for what it does to a march and a battle.
- Resources: where each raw material lies.
handbook.regions_provinces.title: Regions and provinces
handbook.regions_provinces.body:
The world is divided into regions - states, provinces, oblasts as each country calls them - and every region into provinces.

A region is where people live and things are built: its population, peoples and classes, its buildings, deposits and construction, its stability and radicalism. Left click a region to open its card; "Details" opens the full inspector with population and province tabs.

A province is where armies stand and fronts run. It has an owner, a controller (who holds it now), terrain, rivers to cross and the divisions standing in it. When a war moves a border by provinces, the regions it cuts are split into new regions.
handbook.nation_screen.title: Your country
handbook.nation_screen.body:
The country screen is the summary of your state: its capital, regions and people, its economy and its form of government. The Government tab shows the form of government, the ideology in power and how the country is run; Society shows literacy, living standards and the peoples who live there.

Click another country on the map and the same screen shows that country, read-only. The links at the bottom of the screen lead to where each figure is changed.
handbook.budget.title: Budget and taxes
handbook.budget.body:
The Budget screen is where the state's money is decided: what it raises, what it spends and what is left.

## Revenue

Each tax raises money and costs something else: income tax weighs on living standards, corporate tax on investment, value added tax on what people can buy. All of them are charged against the same week's output, so stacking them collects less than their sum. Rest the cursor on a row to see what it raises and what it does.

## Spending

The army and navy, welfare, education, administration, the cost of debt and of everything being built. Military spending decides how large an army the country can keep and how fast it is reinforced. Welfare and education move living standards, literacy and stability slowly, over years.

## If the balance is red

Raise a tax a little, cut what is least needed, or accept the deficit for a while - the treasury can carry it, and after that the state borrows. "Let the treasury run itself" hands the rates to the government's own judgement.
handbook.central_bank.title: The central bank and inflation
handbook.central_bank.body:
The central bank sets the key rate: the price of borrowing for everybody in the country. Four per cent is neutral, twelve is tight, under one is as loose as it goes. Next to it are inflation and the bank's target.

By default the bank is independent and moves the rate itself, against its own target. The line under the card says what it is doing now: raising, cutting or holding.

The government can take the rate away from the bank. That costs nothing by itself; what costs is holding the rate below where the bank wanted it, because cheap money nobody believes in shows up in prices before it shows up anywhere else. The card shows the price in points of inflation a week before you move the slider.

Once the rate is the government's, a second slider appears: printing money. The money arrives in the treasury at once and is paid for twice - in prices, and in trust that lasts long after the press is switched off.
handbook.public_debt.title: Public debt
handbook.public_debt.body:
When the treasury runs dry the state borrows. The Debt tab of the Economy screen shows what it owes, what that costs a week and how far the markets trust it.

The cost of debt rises with how much is owed against the size of the economy and with missed payments. A country that keeps missing payments falls into arrears, then insolvency, then default - and a default is news the whole world reads, with consequences for trade, stability and every loan after it. Restructuring buys time at a price.

The simplest defence is a budget that balances over the years: deficits in a war or a crisis, surpluses after.
handbook.laws.title: Laws, promises and the national course
handbook.laws.body:
The Laws screen holds the rules the country lives by, in categories: administration, civil rights, education, the economy, labour, migration, military service, information, security, social guarantees and more. Only one law of each category is in force at a time.

## Changing a law

Select a category, compare the alternatives on the left with the one in force, and read the effects on the right. Enacting a law costs money and starts a cooling-off period before that category can be changed again. Regional measures apply to one region, foreign doctrines to your dealings with one country.

## Promises

A promise is a public goal with a deadline - lower inflation, more construction, a stronger army. Keeping it earns stability and trust; breaking it costs both.

## The national course

The course is what the country has come to believe over years: shaped by prosperity, war, crises and its government. It changes slowly and pushes back against policies that go against it.
handbook.decisions.title: Decisions and formable nations
handbook.decisions.body:
Decisions are one-off acts a country can take when its situation allows: a reform, a programme, a declaration. Each says what it costs, what it needs and what it does; the situation report counts how many are open to you.

Formable nations are larger states a country can proclaim when it has what they need: the core regions under its control, enough stability, peace on its borders and the money. Some can be formed peacefully, by inviting neighbours who consent. Proclaiming one changes the country's name and flag and keeps its people and history.
handbook.economy_overview.title: Where GDP comes from
handbook.economy_overview.body:
GDP is the value of what the country actually produced in the past year. Buildings in the regions produce goods, workers staff them, the market sets prices from supply and demand, and output times price is the economy.

What follows at the table:

- Industry built where people live pays more than industry built where nobody does: an understaffed factory runs below capacity.
- Taxes, stability, war and shortages do not cut GDP directly. They change productivity, and productivity changes output, a little later.
- A shortage of raw materials or energy shows in the market first and in GDP afterwards.

The Economy screen has four tabs: the week's budget and output, debt, the market and construction.
handbook.market.title: The market and shortages
handbook.market.body:
Every good - food, energy, metals, electronics, arms and the rest - has a price on the world market that follows supply and demand. Each country buys what it lacks and sells what it has spare, through the partners it can reach.

A shortage is the share of demand the country cannot cover. Shortages of essentials lower living standards and stability; shortages of inputs slow the industries that need them. The alert "Shortages" in the situation report opens the market tab, where each good shows production, demand, imports and price.

Goods form chains: bauxite and cheap electricity make aluminium, natural gas becomes fertiliser and fertiliser becomes food, rare earths go into electronics. A break in a chain slows industry with a delay of a week, which is why an embargo bites gradually.
handbook.trade.title: Trade
handbook.trade.body:
Trade has names. Every week your shortages are matched against the spare goods of particular countries, and the result is a list of trade routes on the Trade screen.

Who sells to you is decided by diplomacy: war and embargo close a pair, a trade agreement nearly doubles its pull, an alliance adds to it, hostility and distance reduce it. How much you can bring in is decided by your ports and railways - build them where trade is short.

The trade policy sets how open the country is: open markets for the most imports and exports at low tariffs, balanced trade in the middle, strategic autarky for protection from outside shocks at the price of covering less. A large trading partner has real power over you, and you over it: an embargo is the step between a protest and a war, and it costs both sides.
handbook.production.title: Industry and production lines
handbook.production.body:
The Industry screen shows what the country's factories make and lets you direct the war industry: which equipment, ammunition and vehicles the arms factories turn out, line by line.

Each line takes factory capacity and inputs from the market. Lines without their inputs slow down; lines making what nobody needs waste capacity. In war, what the arms industry produces decides how fast divisions get their equipment back.
handbook.construction.title: Construction
handbook.construction.body:
Buildings are what the economy is made of: industry, agriculture, infrastructure, ports, railways, universities, barracks, arms factories and more. Each is built in a region, takes construction capacity and money, and finishes gradually.

To build, open a region of yours (left click on the map, then Details) or the Construction tab of the Economy screen, and choose what to put up. Before building, check the upkeep and whether the region has the workers for it. Construction capacity that builds nothing is wasted, which is why the situation report warns when nothing is being built.

War damages regions; reconstruction restores them over time.
handbook.research.title: Research
handbook.research.body:
Research points come every week from the country's universities, literacy and economy. They go into one project at a time on the technology tree: industry, society and science, the military and logistics.

A technology needs the ones before it; its card shows what it gives, how many points it costs and roughly how many weeks that is at your pace. Knowledge spreads: a technology your neighbours and partners already have costs you less. Switching projects keeps the points already invested.
handbook.army.title: The army: divisions and recruitment
handbook.army.body:
The army is made of divisions. Each is a unit of its own with men, equipment, experience, organisation and cohesion. Several divisions in one province share one counter on the map: the number on top is how many divisions, the number below how many men.

## Raising divisions

Recruit and deploy on the Army screen. A new division costs money and manpower from the reserve, needs a controlled province to form in, and starts with low organisation. Infantry is slower and holds ground well; motorised and armoured units move and break through faster and use far more supply.

## What a division needs

- Organisation: its ability to fight now. It drops in battle and on the march and recovers at rest.
- Strength and equipment: men and weapons. Reinforcement brings them back from the manpower reserve and the arms industry.
- Supply: food, fuel and ammunition, brought along a chain of friendly provinces.

Militia is raised by threatened regions on their own and defends its home region.
handbook.orders.title: Giving orders and battle plans
handbook.orders.body:
Select divisions with a left click or by dragging a box; the army panel opens on the left with their rows, and the order buttons below.

- Right click on a province: march there. Shift and right click adds a waypoint.
- Halt (H): stop and hold the current province.
- Defend front: take up the threatened border provinces and hold them.
- Advance front: push evenly along the whole front.
- Spearhead: a concentrated thrust towards one province or the war's goal.
- Reserve: stand behind the line, recover faster and join nearby battles.
- Auto-deploy: spread the selected divisions over the front between defence, attack, reserve and spearhead.

## Plans

Divisions with an attack order that stand at the front build up planning, worth up to thirty per cent more attack. Prepare the plan, let it build, then Execute: an immediate attack is faster, a prepared one is stronger. Drawn front lines and plans keep their divisions on their sectors as the front moves.
handbook.supply.title: Supply, reinforcement and encirclement
handbook.supply.body:
Supply comes from the country's inner regions along a chain of provinces you control. Infrastructure and barracks raise how much the chain can carry; too many divisions in one place overload it.

A division cut off from supply loses organisation and strength every day, gets almost no reinforcement, and if the pocket is not broken it surrenders - the men in it become prisoners. Encircling the enemy is the most effective thing an army can do, and being encircled the most costly.

Reinforcement is not free: it comes out of the manpower reserve, is limited per day by mobilisation, money and local supply, and needs the arms industry to replace equipment.
handbook.long_range.title: Long-range forces
handbook.long_range.body:
Artillery brigades, rocket artillery, strike drones, aviation and air defence fight from bases behind the front line. Each formation is based in a region and reaches battles within its range; its card on the map stands at its base.

On the Long-range screen you raise new formations (a region can host two plus two for each barracks), move them between bases, and set their missions: close support of the battles in reach, interdiction of the enemy's rear, air superiority for fighters, or standby. Air defence protects the regions within its reach from enemy aviation and drones.

Long-range formations wear down in use and recover at base. They are expensive, and the most useful thing an army without many divisions can buy.
handbook.navy.title: The navy and landings
handbook.navy.body:
Fleets are listed in the situation report under Navy; click one to open its panel. A fleet has a home port, hulls, strength and experience, and missions: anchored in port, patrol, blockade, raiding enemy shipping, escorting your own, and carrying an invasion.

Divisions can cross the sea: embark them on a fleet in a port, sail, and launch the landing on an enemy coast. A landing against a defended shore is costly, and a fleet that loses control of the sea leaves the landed divisions without supply. New hulls are laid down in shipyards.
handbook.wars.title: War, war score and occupation
handbook.wars.body:
A war is declared from the Diplomacy screen. A country can usually name a reason - land that was taken, its people across the border, a friend it guaranteed; a war without one costs stability, war support and reputation with everyone watching. Allies and guarantors of the country attacked are called in, each with its own declaration.

## Occupation

When a division wins a province, the province changes controller at once and its occupation then secures itself over time. Only securely held ground counts fully at the peace.

## War score

The score runs from -100 to 100 and is made of the ground held, battles won and lost, the war's goal region and how the people at home bear the war. The Wars screen lists every war in the world, its score, fronts and losses; your own come first.
handbook.peace.title: Making peace
handbook.peace.body:
The peace conference is opened from the Wars screen. You paint the peace on the map with the left mouse button: provinces under the brush go into the demand, the right button gives them back, and the map shows the border you are asking for.

## War score is a budget

Every part of a demand has a price. Ground you hold securely costs the base price, ground you hold but have not secured more, ground you never touched most of all; the war's goal region is cheaper, a capital region dearer. Reparations, a trade agreement, disarming the enemy, humiliating it, a long truce and making it your dependency all cost score too. If the demand costs more than the war earned, the other side refuses and says by how much.

## Whole regions

By default a treaty hands over whole regions, so borders follow the map's regions. The campaign option "Peace by provinces" lets every treaty take exactly the provinces it names.

Ready-made terms remain for the common cases: white peace, reparations, keep what is held, capitulation. A peace starts a truce of five years.
handbook.war_weariness.title: Long wars
handbook.war_weariness.body:
No war goes on for ever. From its third year a war weighs on both governments: support for it falls, stability and output suffer, and both sides become readier to accept terms. A war whose score has hardly moved for half a year is a stalemate, and the side that is not winning asks to stop; the peace of a deadlock makes the line the border where anyone holds anything.

A war in which no player fights ends of exhaustion in its eighth year. A player's war is never ended for them, but the other side becomes ever readier to sign.

A state fighting its own breakaway is different: it takes its ground back, never sells it for a white peace while it is winning, and a breakaway that has lost most of its land surrenders whole.
handbook.diplomacy.title: Diplomacy and opinion
handbook.diplomacy.body:
The Diplomacy screen lists every country with what it thinks of you. Find one by name, or filter to allies, rivals, enemies and neighbours. Its page shows how it compares with you, what its opinion is made of, what it has signed and with whom, and what you can do about it.

## Opinion

Opinion runs from -100 to 100 and is the sum of its reasons: a shared border, alliances, wars fought, aid sent, insults, ideology, land taken. Each reason has a size and most fade with time. Rest the cursor on the opinion to see them.

## Actions

- Improve relations: a mission that costs money and buys goodwill for a while.
- Denounce: say in public what you think of them.
- Propose an alliance, guarantee their independence, sign a trade agreement or a non-aggression pact.
- Send aid, or impose an embargo.
- Offer protection, buy influence or back a government: ways to make a smaller country answer to you.
- Declare war, issue an ultimatum, or negotiate peace.

Each button says what it costs and, where the answer can be known, what the answer will be.
handbook.alliances.title: Alliances, guarantees and coalitions
handbook.alliances.body:
An alliance is a promise to fight: when one ally is attacked, each of the others is asked to join, and an ally that refuses loses the alliance in public. The world opens with the alliances that were in force in 2024 - NATO, the CSTO and the rest.

An alliance has cohesion. Shared enemies and kept promises hold it together; diverging interests, unanswered calls and long neglect wear it down until it breaks. Alliance programmes - joint exercises, arms deliveries, help in a crisis - strengthen it for money.

A guarantee is the cheap half of an alliance: it costs nothing until the guaranteed country is attacked.

A coalition gathers against a country that takes too much by force. Notoriety from conquest is counted by the people taken, fades only with time, and while it is high the whole world thinks worse of the conqueror.
handbook.subjects.title: Dependencies
handbook.movements.title: Movements
handbook.movements.body:
Movements are countries without land: Hamas, the Central Tibetan Administration, the Order of Malta, independence campaigns, governments in exile. They have a headquarters in a host country, money, cadres, support in the regions they care about, and a government of their own. Each is shown on the map by its headquarters badge; click it for its page.

A movement acts: it organises, raises money, wins support, negotiates, and, if it is armed, can rise in a region where its support is strong. A rising that takes ground turns the movement into a country at war with the state it rose against. A civic movement campaigns for a vote instead.

What you can do about a movement in your country: talk to it, crack down on it, or designate it. Each has a price in stability and in what the world thinks of you.

When a country is conquered outright its government may go into exile as a movement and keep fighting for its return.
handbook.stability.title: Stability and unrest
handbook.stability.body:
A country's stability is worked out from its regions and its capital: how people live, whether they think of the state as theirs, how they are governed, war, prices and shortages. Rest the cursor on Stability in the top bar for its reasons.

Each region has its own stability and radicalism. Radicalism grows with poverty, unemployment, war on the region's ground, a foreign government and broken promises, and falls with prosperity, good administration and time.

What low stability does: taxes collect less, output falls, militia raise less readily, movements win support, and a region that is angry, ungoverned and not the state's own people may break away. Living standards, welfare and education spending, laws on rights and administration, and peace are the slow cures; promises and decisions the quick ones.
handbook.secession.title: Secession and breakaway states
handbook.secession.body:
A region breaks away when four things are true at once: its people are not the state's own, it is angry, it has stopped being governed, and the state looks unable to stop it. None of them alone is enough. Neighbouring regions that are angry and ungoverned enough may go with it.

What comes out is a country with a name, a flag, a capital and an army - its militia, and part of the garrison that stood there. The state it left either lets it go or goes to war to keep it; a player's country is asked.

A state fighting its breakaway is taking back its own ground: it pays a fraction of the usual price for it at the peace, does not trade it for a white peace while it is winning, and takes it back whole when the breakaway surrenders. A breakaway surrenders once most of its land is held or nobody in it still believes in the war.
handbook.population.title: Peoples, classes and minorities
handbook.population.body:
Population lives in regions, in groups by people and by class, each with an occupation, an income, a standard of living and a mood. A region's Population tab shows them.

People do not change their nationality with a treaty. A region taken by force is full of people who did not choose it: more radical than its neighbours, and it stays so for a generation. Assimilation is slow and depends on conditions - faster where people are educated and live well, slower where they are angry.

Literacy and living standards rise with education and welfare spending and with growth, and they decide much of what a country can produce and how settled it is.
handbook.reputation.title: Reputation and the established normal
handbook.reputation.body:
The section "Public reputation" on a country's diplomacy page is what particular societies think of it: each audience - a country, a people, a coalition - holds its own view. Public acts leave a fading memory: wars, aid, crackdowns, broken treaties. A view held long enough settles into admiration or stigma, and both take years to change back. Reputation feeds into opinion, into readiness for alliances and into a movement's support.

"The established normal" is what a country's people have got used to. Institutions and borders that last become trusted; a crisis, an occupation or a change of government stops that trust settling. Living standards set expectations: prosperity that people are used to is expected to continue, and losing it costs stability.
handbook.reports.title: Reports and charts
handbook.reports.body:
The Reports screen is the statistical office: charts of GDP, the treasury, population, stability and living standards, the budget week by week, the market, the armed forces and the wars, world rankings and the chronicle of everything that has happened.

History is recorded once a week and kept for fifteen years. Rest the cursor on a line or a bar for the exact day, value and explanation. "Map selection" switches the charts to the country last selected on the map, so any two countries can be compared.
handbook.tensions.title: Tensions and incidents
handbook.tensions.body:
Between peace and war there is tension: a figure from 0 to 100 for each pair of countries with a reason for it. It moves towards where its reasons put it - hostility, a grievance from past wars, land one holds of the other's, a declared rivalry, wars in which the two back opposite sides, and for some pairs a standing dispute no week of good behaviour removes, like the armistice line in Korea. Neighbours feel all of it; countries far apart feel less; alliances, pacts and trade soften it.

## The stages

- Friction, from 25: diplomats expelled, airspace violated, a cyber attack.
- Crisis, from 50: sabotage, an assassination.
- Armed clashes, from 75: shooting across the border every week, artillery duels and raids. Both sides lose men and rally behind their armies. Only armed clashes count in the computer's case for a war.

## Border wars

A shared border that has been shooting for three months can turn into a border war: a few weeks of real fighting between the two alone, with nobody's allies called, ended by a ceasefire on the old lines - as between India and Pakistan in May 2025. Whoever refuses the ceasefire when it falls due has an ordinary war on their hands.

Incidents become likelier the higher the tension and are reported in the news. Each moves the tension again and is remembered in the opinion of the country it was done to.

## After a war

The side that lost provinces and soldiers keeps a grievance that halves only in about thirty years, and while it lasts it holds the tension up. That is how one war's peace becomes the cause of the next.

## Bringing it down

Open the Conflicts screen, choose the standoff and hold talks: four months during which tension falls every week. Treaties, trade and better opinion lower it for good.

## Wars grow too

A war becomes a major war after five months and heavy losses, and a total war after fourteen months and very heavy ones. A larger war calls up more men, wears both economies harder and makes any compromise harder to accept.
handbook.proxy_wars.title: Backing other people's wars
handbook.proxy_wars.body:
A country can back one side of a war it is not fighting: the Conflicts screen, a war, "Back a side". The support has three levels - advisers and money, weapons, weapons at scale with volunteers - and costs a weekly share of the sponsor's economy; a small economy can only give the first.

What the client gets: part of the payment as money in its treasury, the rest as weapons that re-equip its most worn divisions, volunteers at the highest level, and a modifier on its army for as long as the support lasts. What the sponsor gets is the war going the way it wants without a declaration - and the lasting anger of the side it arms against, whose tension with it rises every week. Two powers backing opposite sides of one war are in a proxy confrontation.

The world opens with the backers of 2024: the United States, Britain, Germany, Poland and others arming Ukraine; Iran, North Korea and Belarus supplying Russia. The computer backs the side it likes against the side it does not, sooner when a rival of its own backs the other side, when the war is next door, or when the client is its ally or dependency, and it stops when the case fades or the money runs out.

handbook.factions.title: De facto powers
handbook.factions.body:
Some of the countries on the map are not recognised states. On 1 January 2024 a number of real organisations held and governed ground of their own: the Rapid Support Forces in Darfur and Khartoum, the Houthis' Ansar Allah in Sanaa and the north-west of Yemen, the Syrian Salvation Government in Idlib, the Syrian Interim Government in the Turkish-held north, North and East Syria beyond the Euphrates, the Libyan National Army in the east and south of Libya, Myanmar's National Unity Government, Arakan Army and Kachin Independence Organisation, al-Shabaab in the Juba valley and the Alliance Fleuve Congo around the M23 in North Kivu. They start as what they were: countries with land, an army of their own, and a war, a truce or a peace with the state whose ground they hold.

## What they can do

They are played by the computer like any other country, and you can play one. The dossier of each says who it is, whose ground it holds and who backs it.

## Their wars

A war between a state and its de facto power is a civil war. Only the two sides fight in it: their friends back them with money and weapons (see "Backing other people's wars"), and no ally or coalition is called. A state that wins can write the ground back in whole; a faction that loses most of its ground fights on while it still has an army and people who believe in the war.

## Their patrons

Some are kept going by a foreign state - the United Arab Emirates and the Rapid Support Forces, Iran and the Houthis, Russia and the Libyan National Army, the United States in north-eastern Syria. A country thinking of attacking a faction counts its patrons' strength against itself. A state that lists a faction as a terrorist or sanctioned organisation never arms it.
handbook.coups.title: Coups and the fall of governments
handbook.coups.body:
Governments of the 2020s ended in coups far more often than by conquest: Myanmar, Mali, Guinea, Sudan, Burkina Faso twice, Niger and Gabon in four years.

## The plot

Below 35% stability officers may start plotting against the government - the lower it falls, the likelier - most of all against a military junta or a provisional government, when a war is being lost, or in the years after a coup next door. A parliament or a crown is far harder to overthrow.

A plot takes two months to ripen. If stability is back above 35% by then, the plot comes to nothing. If not, the army takes power: the country becomes a military junta, with a brief order of its own and the coldness of the liberal, social-democratic and conservative governments of the world.

## When it is yours

The situation rail warns you the day officers begin plotting, and the country's dossier shows the coup risk at any time. What raises stability raises it in time: spending on welfare and order, laws, ending a war that is being lost.

## The fall of a capital

A de facto power that means to rule the whole country - the Rapid Support Forces, the Houthis, Myanmar's National Unity Government - and holds the government's capital and half its ground takes the state: all of it, its name and its seat. The government that fell goes into exile or is gone.
